title: Principles of Flight
summary: Connect airflow, energy, stability, and load to what the pilot actually feels and controls.
objectives: Explain lift and stall without equal-transit-time or zero-lift myths.
Predict how speed, load, and drag change together.
Connect stability, propeller effects, and wake behavior to practical risk management.

sections.title: Forces, airflow, and lift production
sections.body:
Weight acts toward Earth. Aerodynamic lift is defined perpendicular to the relative airflow, while drag acts opposite the aircraft’s motion through that airflow. Lift is not defined perpendicular to the chord line and does not always point vertically upward. Thrust generally acts near the propeller or engine axis. In steady, unaccelerated flight, the vector sum of the forces is zero even during a steady climb or descent.

A wing turns airflow and produces a pressure distribution around its surfaces. The pressure forces on the wing and the momentum change in the air describe the same interaction. Bernoulli’s relationship and Newton’s laws are compatible descriptions; the air divided at the leading edge has no requirement to reunite at the trailing edge.
sections.deep:
The useful equation: lift equals dynamic pressure times wing area times lift coefficient. Here V is speed relative to the air, not groundspeed. Shape, angle of attack, configuration, and flow conditions influence Cₗ. A cambered airfoil can make positive lift at zero geometric angle of attack. More speed or wing area can increase lift without changing that geometric angle.

L=12ρV2SCL

In a simple steady climb with thrust aligned with the flight path, part of weight acts along the path and lift balances the perpendicular component. “Climbing means lift is greater than weight” is therefore an unreliable general explanation.

sections.title: Angle of attack, separation, and stall
sections.body:
Angle of attack is the angle between an airfoil’s chord reference and the relative airflow. It is different from pitch attitude, which compares the aircraft with the horizon. A wing can reach its critical angle with a high or low nose attitude and at many airspeeds.

As angle of attack rises, lift coefficient generally increases until the wing reaches its maximum usable coefficient. Extensive flow separation then reduces lift capability and increases drag. A stalled wing still produces aerodynamic force; it has not suddenly lost all lift. Recovery requires reducing angle of attack below the critical value, with the remaining actions and limitations taken from the aircraft procedures.
sections.deep:
Why indicated stall speed varies: speed is the amount of airflow needed to produce the required lift with the available maximum coefficient. Higher weight or load requires more lift and therefore more speed at that limit. Flaps, contamination, or a changed wing shape can change both the lift curve and the critical angle. A universal critical angle such as “16 degrees for every airplane” is not a valid operational limit.

Flaps often increase maximum lift coefficient and reduce stall speed, even if the geometric angle at stall decreases. Ice can degrade the curve and warning margin in ways a clean-wing demonstration does not predict.

sections.title: Drag and the energy required to climb
sections.body:
Parasite drag includes shape, skin-friction, and interference effects. At otherwise fixed conditions, it rises strongly as airspeed increases. Induced drag is associated with producing lift with a finite wing. For a fixed lift requirement, lower speed requires a larger lift coefficient and usually more induced drag. Combining those trends produces a minimum-drag region.

A sustainable climb needs energy in excess of that used to overcome drag. Raising the nose can initially trade kinetic energy for altitude, but that exchange cannot sustain the climb indefinitely. Power is the rate of energy transfer: the speed for maximum excess power produces the best rate of climb, while maximum excess thrust relates to best climb angle.
sections.deep:
Deeper relationship: the drag polar separates a baseline term from a lift-dependent term. Combining it with the lift equation makes the fixed-lift speed dependence visible.

CD=CD0+kCL2Di=2kL2ρV2S

At fixed lift, induced drag is proportional to 1/V². Parasite drag grows approximately with V². The minimum of total drag identifies maximum lift-to-drag ratio in the model; minimum power occurs at a different speed.

Ground effect changes the wing’s induced-flow pattern and can reduce induced drag near the surface. It does not create energy. An aircraft that accelerates in ground effect may still lack the excess power to climb safely away. Published performance and configuration limits govern the real decision.

sections.title: Bank, load factor, and the flight envelope
sections.body:
In a coordinated, constant-altitude turn, the vertical component of lift must still balance weight. Banking directs another component inward to curve the flight path. Total lift must therefore increase. The ratio L/W is load factor, n. For this specific model, the load factor is the reciprocal of the cosine of bank. At 60 degrees, n = 2: total lift is twice weight.

n=LW=1cosφVSn=VS1n

With weight, configuration, and maximum lift coefficient fixed, stall speed rises as the square root of load factor. A 50-knot one-g stall speed becomes about 71 knots at two g. Bank alone does not impose that load in every maneuver; unloading or allowing a descent changes the force requirement.
sections.deep:
Why the envelope matters: a V–g diagram combines aerodynamic stall boundaries with structural load and speed limits. At high speed, a sharp control input may reach a structural limit before a protective stall occurs. At low speed, an accelerated stall can occur well above the familiar one-g stall speed.

Use the actual AFM/POH category, loading restrictions, maneuvering speeds, and limitations. Historical normal- and utility-category figures are examples, not universal permissions. Ultimate load is a certification-strength margin beyond limit load, not an extra pilot operating allowance. Maneuvering speed also does not protect against every gust, repeated control input, or combined-axis loading.

sections.title: Static stability, damping, and center of gravity
sections.body:
Static stability describes the initial response to a disturbance: toward the original condition, no restoring tendency, or farther away. Dynamic stability describes what happens over time. A response can initially restore but still oscillate with increasing amplitude. Positive damping removes energy from the oscillation; neutral damping sustains it and negative damping increases it.

Pitch stability depends on the whole aircraft, including the wing, tail, fuselage, downwash, power, and center of gravity. Moving the CG aft generally reduces the restoring pitch tendency and changes control-force and recovery margins. Moving it forward can increase the tail force and control authority required for takeoff and landing.
sections.deep:
A better deeper model: compare CG with the aircraft’s neutral point, rather than treating a moving “center of lift” as a universal hinge. A conventional aircraft often uses a downward tail force in a particular trimmed condition, but that is not a universal rule for every configuration and maneuver.

Dihedral and related geometry couple sideslip into roll; the vertical tail provides directional restoring effects. These mechanisms do not guarantee that every roll–yaw mode is well damped. Remaining inside the approved CG envelope protects the tested balance of stability and control. “Aft CG is always unrecoverable” overstates the issue; the serious concern is the reduced margin and potentially inadequate recovery outside approved limits.

sections.title: Why propeller effects change with the maneuver
sections.body:
For a typical clockwise-turning propeller viewed from the cockpit, torque reaction tends to roll the aircraft left. Spiraling slipstream can strike the vertical tail and yaw the nose left. At a positive angle between propeller axis and relative airflow, unequal blade loading can shift thrust toward the descending side of the disc, creating P-factor yaw.

A spinning propeller also has angular momentum. Changing the orientation of that rotating system creates gyroscopic effects whose direction depends on propeller rotation and the applied pitch or yaw change. A tailwheel airplane raising its tail is a useful example, but a memorized “always left” rule cannot describe every maneuver or opposite-rotating propeller.
sections.deep:
Why power and airspeed matter: high power increases propeller-related forces while low airspeed can reduce the effectiveness of aerodynamic controls. A nose-high, high-power climb can therefore need more coordination input than cruise. The correct input is the amount that produces the required aircraft response, not a fixed pedal position recalled from another flight.

The rudder counters yaw and manages sideslip; the ailerons primarily control roll. Avoid explaining torque roll as though the rudder directly cancels an equal roll moment. Aircraft rigging, trim, propeller direction, and the current maneuver determine how those effects combine. Teach the causes separately before discussing their combined cockpit symptoms.

sections.title: Wake turbulence and the limits of prediction
sections.body:
A finite wing producing lift leaves a rotating wake. The strongest hazardous wakes are associated with heavy, clean, slow aircraft. A following light aircraft may not have enough roll control to oppose an encounter. Vortices initially descend and can drift with the wind; near the ground they can spread laterally. A light crosswind may keep one vortex near the runway while moving the other away.

Plan avoidance around the preceding aircraft’s actual flight path, rotation point, touchdown point, wind, and the available runway. In suitable same-runway situations, staying above its approach path and landing beyond its touchdown, or rotating before its rotation point and climbing above its path, can help.
sections.deep:
Why those rules need judgment: the preceding path may be unknown, an intersecting runway may produce a different encounter, and the following aircraft may not be able to outclimb the leader. Wake does not follow a perfectly timed elevator down through the air. Terrain, wind shear, atmospheric conditions, and aircraft behavior change its location and persistence.

Request more spacing or delay when the avoidance geometry is uncertain. Comply with applicable separation requirements, but do not assume that the passage of a minimum interval proves the wake is gone. Wake is linked to lift production, not solely to aircraft engine operation or the sound of a departing jet.

teachBack: Explain why a cambered airfoil can lift at zero geometric angle of attack without relying on equal transit time.
Derive n = 1/cos φ for a level turn and explain which assumptions make the equation valid.
Explain how a forward and aft CG can create different control problems, using the actual aircraft envelope.
takeaways: Lift direction is defined by relative airflow, not the chord line.
Critical angle and indicated stall speed describe different things.
A climb consumes energy at a rate; pitching up alone cannot sustain it.
Load factor changes stall speed and structural margin.
Wake behavior is a planning problem with uncertainty.

quiz.question: A cambered airfoil produces positive lift at zero geometric angle of attack. Which explanation is consistent with aerodynamic principles?
options: The lift equation must fail at zero angle.
Its shape can produce a nonzero lift coefficient at that angle.
The air above and below must take equal travel times.
Its lift must point perpendicular to the chord instead of the airflow.
feedback: The equation accommodates a nonzero lift coefficient at zero geometric angle.
Camber can shift the angle at which lift coefficient is zero.
Equal transit time is not a condition required by the airflow.
Lift is defined perpendicular to relative airflow regardless of the chord orientation.
quiz.hint: Separate geometric angle from the lift coefficient produced by the airfoil.

quiz.question: In a coordinated, constant-altitude 60-degree bank, an aircraft has a 50-knot one-g stall speed. With configuration and weight unchanged, what is the approximate two-g stall speed, rounded to the nearest knot?
options: 50 knots
100 knots
71 knots
35 knots
feedback: One-g stall speed does not satisfy the greater lift requirement at two g.
Stall speed scales with the square root of load factor rather than directly with it.
50 times the square root of 2 is about 70.71, which rounds to 71 knots.
Greater required lift raises rather than lowers stall speed in this model.
quiz.hint: First find load factor from the bank, then apply the square-root relationship.

quiz.question: During an aerodynamic stall, which change is essential to restore attached-flow capability?
options: Reduce angle of attack below the critical value.
Keep increasing back pressure until the nose rises.
Wait for the engine to reach maximum rpm before changing angle.
Level the wings while holding the stalled angle unchanged.
feedback: Reducing angle of attack addresses the aerodynamic cause of the stall.
Additional back pressure can maintain or deepen the stalled condition.
Power can help recovery but does not replace the required angle-of-attack reduction.
Wing leveling alone does not remove excessive angle of attack.
quiz.hint: Identify the variable that defines the stall itself.

quiz.question: In the ideal model, lift and configuration stay fixed while airspeed increases. What happens to induced drag?
options: It rises with the square of speed.
It stays constant because lift stays constant.
It becomes zero as soon as the aircraft is fast.
It decreases because the required lift coefficient decreases.
feedback: That trend describes the simplified parasite-drag term, not fixed-lift induced drag.
Maintaining lift at higher speed reduces the required lift coefficient and induced-drag contribution.
A finite wing producing lift still has an induced-drag contribution.
Substitution of the lift equation gives induced drag proportional to lift squared divided by speed squared.
quiz.hint: Consider how much lift coefficient is needed at the higher dynamic pressure.

quiz.question: Moving the CG aft toward the whole-aircraft neutral point generally has which effect?
options: It necessarily makes every stall unrecoverable.
It reduces the restoring pitch-stability margin.
It guarantees a larger safe loading envelope.
It removes the need to follow the AFM/POH CG limits.
feedback: Recovery depends on the aircraft and condition; the universal statement is too strong.
The separation between CG and neutral point is a useful measure of longitudinal static-stability margin.
The approved envelope is set by the aircraft’s demonstrated limits, not by a desired handling change.
Aft loading can reduce important control and recovery margins, so limits remain essential.
quiz.hint: Use the aircraft’s restoring tendency rather than a universal center-of-lift hinge.

quiz.question: A light airplane follows a heavy, clean aircraft on final with a light crosswind. Which plan best reflects wake uncertainty?
options: Assume the crosswind immediately clears both vortices.
Descend below the leader’s path to avoid its sinking wake.
Consider its path and touchdown point, stay above when appropriate, and request more spacing if uncertain.
Use the leader’s engine noise to determine whether vortices still exist.
feedback: A light crosswind can keep one vortex near the runway.
Descending below the path can place the follower into the descending wake.
The plan uses encounter geometry and retains the option to increase separation.
Wake is associated with lift production rather than a dependable engine-noise cue.
quiz.hint: Think about where the vortices can move relative to the following aircraft.
